goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb:36 persists feed HTML with raw_html, bypassing sanitization and enabling stored XSS from malicious feed items

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb line 36, the code does `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`. In TopicEmbed.import (app/models/topic_embed.rb), the content is passed to PostCreator with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. In app/models/post.rb, when cook_method is raw_html, the cook method returns `raw` directly without any sanitization: `return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. The content from RSS feeds (i.content) is only processed with CGI.unescapeHTML and .scrub, but no HTML sanitization. This means malicious JavaScript in RSS feed items would be stored and rendered directly, creating a stored XSS vulnerability. The finding correctly identifies that raw_html bypasses sanitization for feed content.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:44 validates only the initial URL host while open-uri follows redirects, allowing an approved-host redirect to access private or internal addresses and cause SSRF

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 44-47, the import_remote method uses `open(url).read` to fetch content from a URL. The URL validation only checks if it starts with 'http://' or 'https://' (line 11: `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`). In lib/topic_retriever.rb, the invalid_host? method checks if `SiteSetting.embeddable_host != URI(@embed_url).host`, but this check happens before the HTTP request. The actual HTTP fetch in import_remote uses Ruby's open-uri which follows redirects by default. An attacker could provide a URL on the approved embeddable_host that redirects to an internal/private address, bypassing the host validation. This is a legitimate SSRF vulnerability because the host check validates the initial URL but open-uri will follow redirects to arbitrary destinations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:46 imports raw HTML sanitized by ruby-readability 0.5.7 without filtering dangerous URI schemes, allowing javascript: links and stored click-triggered XSS

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, TopicEmbed.import_remote (line 46-51) uses ruby-readability to parse HTML content with specific allowed tags and attributes: tags: %w[div p code pre h1 h2 h3 b em i strong a img], attributes: %w[href src]. The parsed content is then passed to TopicEmbed.import which stores it with cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html], meaning the raw HTML is rendered directly without further processing (as seen in post.rb lines 131-133: 'return raw if cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]'). Ruby-readability's tag/attribute filtering does allow 'a' tags with 'href' attributes, but it doesn't filter URI schemes. This means javascript: URIs in href attributes would pass through, enabling stored XSS when users click the links. The finding correctly identifies that dangerous URI schemes like javascript: are not filtered, which is a real security vulnerability.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb:3 adds a non-null column with a default, which can rewrite and exclusively lock the posts table and cause significant production downtime

adjudication.rationale: The migration in db/migrate/20131219203905_add_cook_method_to_posts.rb adds a column with `default: 1, null: false`. In older versions of PostgreSQL (before 11), adding a NOT NULL column with a default value requires rewriting the entire table and holding an exclusive lock, which can cause significant downtime on large tables like 'posts'. This is a legitimate concern for production databases. However, the severity depends on the PostgreSQL version and table size. The finding correctly identifies a potential production issue with the migration approach.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb:7 limits embed_url to 255 characters, causing insertion failures for longer successfully fetched article URLs

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the migration file db/migrate/20131217174004_create_topic_embeds.rb, the embed_url column is defined as `t.string :embed_url, null: false`. In Rails, a string column without an explicit limit defaults to 255 characters in most databases. However, the finding claims line 7 'limits embed_url to 255 characters' - but looking at the actual code, there is no explicit limit specified. The default behavior depends on the database adapter. More importantly, URLs can indeed exceed 255 characters, and the code in TopicEmbed.import and other places accepts URLs without length validation. This could cause database insertion failures for long URLs. However, the finding incorrectly states that line 7 explicitly limits to 255 characters when it doesn't - it's just using the default string type. The underlying concern about URL length is valid but the specific claim about the code is imprecise. The migration doesn't explicitly set a 255 character limit; it uses the default string type which may or may not have that limit depending on the database.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:63 incorrectly treats scheme-relative links as root-relative, producing malformed URLs such as https://article-host/cdn.example.com/image.png

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the code in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 54-72, the absolutize_urls method checks if href/src start_with?('/') and then prepends the prefix. However, scheme-relative URLs like '//cdn.example.com/image.png' also start with '/', so they would be incorrectly transformed to 'https://article-host//cdn.example.com/image.png' (with the double slash being treated as a path). The code should check for '//' specifically to avoid mangling protocol-relative URLs. This is a real bug in the URL handling logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:63 does not absolutize path-relative links, causing them to resolve against the Discourse topic or embed URL instead of the source article

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the absolutize_urls method in app/models/topic_embed.rb lines 52-70, the code checks if href/src start_with?('/') and then prepends the prefix. However, the code handles URLs starting with '/' (absolute paths like '/hello') but does NOT handle truly relative URLs (like 'hello' or '../hello' without a leading slash). The test in the spec shows contents with '/hello' and '/images/wat.jpg' which both start with '/', so those are handled. But if the source article had a link like 'relative-page.html' (no leading slash), it would not be absolutized. The finding claims 'path-relative links' are not handled - this is accurate for relative paths that don't start with '/'. However, looking at the actual test case, it only tests paths starting with '/', so the code works for those. The finding is technically correct that truly relative URLs (without leading /) would not be absolutized, which is a real bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:17 uses embed URLs verbatim for lookup, throttling, and uniqueness, so fragment variants of the same HTTP resource create duplicate topics

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, TopicEmbed.import uses embed_url directly for lookup via `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and TopicEmbed.topic_id_for_embed uses `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: embed_url).pluck(:topic_id).first`. The URLs are stored and compared as-is without any normalization. If the same page is accessed with different URL fragments (e.g., 'http://example.com/page' vs 'http://example.com/page#section'), these would be treated as different URLs and could create duplicate topics. Similarly, trailing slashes, query parameter ordering, or case differences in the path could cause duplicates. This is a real correctness issue - the code doesn't normalize URLs before comparison, which could lead to duplicate topic creation for what is essentially the same content.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/embed_controller.rb:15 enqueues jobs for missing embeds before throttling, allowing concurrent requests or repeated reloads to flood the queue with duplicate jobs

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the embed_controller.rb code, when a topic_id is not found for an embed_url, it enqueues a RetrieveTopic job. The TopicRetriever class does have throttling via retrieved_recently? which uses Redis setnx with a 60-second expiry. However, the controller enqueues the job BEFORE any throttling check happens - the throttling is inside the job's execute method via TopicRetriever. This means if a user rapidly reloads the loading page (which auto-reloads every 30 seconds per loading.html.erb), multiple jobs will be enqueued to Sidekiq before the first job even starts executing and sets the Redis throttle key. The finding correctly identifies that jobs are enqueued before throttling, which could lead to duplicate jobs in the queue, especially with concurrent requests or rapid reloads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/topic_retriever.rb:42 synchronously downloads and processes the entire configured feed for every distinct unknown embed URL, with no feed-wide throttle or unchanged-feed check

adjudication.rationale: Looking at lib/topic_retriever.rb:42, the perform_retrieve method checks if feed_polling_enabled? and if so calls Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({}). Looking at app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, the poll_feed method downloads the entire RSS feed and iterates through all items, calling TopicEmbed.import for each. The retrieved_recently? check in topic_retriever.rb only throttles per embed_url (line 26: retrieved_key = "retrieved:#{@embed_url}"), not per feed. So if multiple different unknown embed URLs come in, each one will trigger a full feed download and processing. This is a real performance/resource issue - there's no feed-wide throttle to prevent repeatedly downloading and processing the same feed for different embed URLs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:143 requires fetching every original article during import and does not handle open-uri failures, so a timeout, 404, or similar error aborts the entire Disqus import

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for lib/tasks/disqus.thor, line 143 shows `post = TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`. The import_remote method in app/models/topic_embed.rb uses `open(url).read` without any error handling. If the URL fetch fails (timeout, 404, network error), an exception would be raised. However, this is wrapped in `if options[:dry_run].blank?` and the code continues with `if post.present?` check, suggesting partial handling. But the actual exception from open-uri would indeed abort the import process since there's no rescue block around the import_remote call. This is a real issue - a single failed URL fetch would crash the entire Disqus import process.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:143 drops the exported thread's created_at when replacing PostCreator, assigning current timestamps to imported topics and corrupting historical ordering

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for lib/tasks/disqus.thor, the old code at line 144 had: `creator = PostCreator.new(user, title: t[:title], raw: "\[[Permalink](#{t[:link]})\]", created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at]), category: category_id)` which included `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])`. The new code at line 143 replaces this with: `post = TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`. Looking at TopicEmbed.import_remote, it calls TopicEmbed.import which uses PostCreator without passing created_at. This means the original thread's created_at timestamp is indeed dropped, and imported topics will get current timestamps instead of their historical dates. This is a real functional regression that corrupts historical ordering of imported Disqus threads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:34 ignores title for existing embeds, preventing corrected RSS or article titles from propagating to Discourse topics

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the import method in topic_embed.rb, when an embed already exists (lines 30-38), the code only updates the content if content_sha1 differs, but it never updates the topic title. The title parameter is passed to the method but ignored for existing embeds. For new embeds, the title is used in PostCreator (line 21), but for updates, only the content is revised via PostRevisor (lines 33-35). This means if an RSS feed or article title is corrected, the Discourse topic title will never be updated. This is a real functional limitation/bug in the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:12 validates URLs using only a string-prefix check, allowing malformed values such as http:// to be stored and causing values such as http:// bad to raise later and abort the feed job

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, in app/models/topic_embed.rb line 12, the import method checks `return unless url =~ /^https?\:\/\//`. This regex only checks that the URL starts with 'http://' or 'https://', but doesn't validate the full URL structure. A URL like 'http://' alone would pass this check but would fail later when trying to parse it with URI(). However, looking at the code flow, the URL is used with URI() in absolutize_urls method (line 52-53) which would raise URI::InvalidURIError for malformed URLs. The finding claims this could 'abort the feed job' - looking at poll_feed.rb, the import is called in a loop over RSS items, and an exception would indeed abort processing of remaining items. However, the regex `^https?\:\/\/` actually requires at least 'http://' which is 7 characters, and 'http://' alone is technically a valid URI prefix. The real issue is that malformed URLs like 'http:// bad' (with space) would pass the regex but fail URI parsing. This is a real bug - insufficient URL validation that could cause runtime errors.
